title: Why some flames are blue and others are yellow
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why is a gas flame blue?
Why is a candle flame yellow?

faq.q: Why is a gas flame blue?
faq.a: Gas on a cooker is mixed with air before it burns, so it burns completely without soot. Excited molecules in the flame give out mostly blue light.
asks: Why are gas cooker flames blue?

faq.q: Why is a candle flame yellow?
faq.a: A candle flame does not get enough oxygen mixed in, so tiny soot particles form. They are so hot that they glow yellow, which is what you see.

faq.q: Is a blue flame hotter than a yellow flame?
faq.a: Usually yes. A roaring blue Bunsen flame reaches about 1,500 degrees Celsius, while the yellow safety flame is closer to 1,000 degrees, because burning is more complete with more oxygen.

faq.q: Why does a Bunsen burner change colour when you open the air hole?
faq.a: Opening the hole lets air mix with the gas before it burns. With enough oxygen, no soot forms, so the yellow glow disappears and the flame turns blue.
asks: What does the air hole on a Bunsen do?

faq.q: Why do some flames burn green or purple?
faq.a: Certain metals in the fuel give out their own colours when heated: copper gives green or blue, sodium orange-yellow and potassium lilac. Fireworks use the same trick.

facts: The yellow glow of a candle comes from soot particles heated to over 1,000 degrees Celsius.
A Bunsen burner with its air hole fully open makes a blue flame of about 1,500 degrees Celsius at its hottest point.
